analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay workers sent home with flu symptoms for up to five days.
analysis.headline: The bill was never brought to a vote: after introduction in November 2009 it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee and expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic, this bill would have required employers with 15 or more workers to pay employees sent home (or told not to come in) because they had symptoms of a contagious illness, such as H1N1. The paid leave would be capped at 5 days per year, and employers who already provided at least 5 paid sick days would be exempt. It also made it illegal to fire or discipline a worker for following such a direction or for filing a complaint, with enforcement through the Fair Labor Standards Act's wage-and-hour penalty system. It would have sunset after two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 15 or more employees who lack their own paid sick leave: they could stay home with the flu or after exposure to it without losing pay, up to 5 days a year. Customers and co-workers also benefit indirectly, because workers no longer face a choice between coming to work contagious or losing income. Workers already covered by an employer policy of 5 or more paid sick days, and employees of very small firms, are outside the bill's requirements.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an employer that directs an employee to leave work or stay home over contagious-illness symptoms (or exposure to them) to pay the employee for each workday missed, up to 5 days per 12-month period, at the regular rate of pay [S2, S3].

Makes it unlawful for an employer to discharge, discipline, or discriminate against an employee who complies with such a direction, files a complaint, or testifies in an enforcement proceeding, with penalties tied to the Fair Labor Standards Act [S2, S3].

The stated purpose is to let workers follow employer and public health authority recommendations to stay home without financial harm during a contagious-disease outbreak, specifically including the novel H1N1 virus [S2, S3].

The bill does not reduce existing protections: it preserves any stronger rights under other federal, state, or local law, collective bargaining agreements, or employer policy, and employers that already provide 5 or more discretionary paid sick days per year are exempt [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees that do not already offer at least 5 paid sick days would bear the wage cost when they send sick or exposed workers home, plus compliance costs for posting notices and following Labor Department guidelines. In service industries with many hourly workers, the cost of paying workers not at work would fall on businesses.

drawbacks.text: The requirement is narrow: it only triggers pay when the employer directs the worker to leave, so a worker who stays home on a doctor's or health department's advice without the employer's direction may still go unpaid, limiting the bill's public-health reach [S2, S3].

Employers bear new costs with little lead time: the bill would have taken effect no later than 15 days after enactment and would have required immediate compliance plus Labor Department guidance, a burden critics of the bill's general approach (a new paid-leave mandate) typically cite for small and low-margin service businesses [S3].
The 5-day-per-year cap and the employer's ability to end the leave once it believes the employee is no longer contagious give employers substantial discretion over when paid leave stops [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real problem in the middle of a pandemic: many hourly workers could not afford to miss a shift, so they came to work sick and exposed co-workers and customers. Its costs are real but bounded — pay only when the employer sends the worker home, capped at 5 days a year, with employers already offering 5 sick days exempt — and it expires after two years. The main design weakness is that it leaves the trigger in the employer's hands rather than the worker's or a doctor's, which narrows who is protected.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced, then to a subcommittee a month later, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) introduced the bill on November 3, 2009, during the H1N1 pandemic, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which he chaired [S1, S5].

On December 8, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no Senate action for the rest of the 111th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 12 cosponsors, all Democrats in a House where Democrats held 253 of 435 seats, and died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2011, without ever reaching the floor [S1, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers without existing paid sick leave policies avoided a new wage mandate during a pandemic, and businesses in heavily affected service sectors avoided the cost of paying workers they sent home. Workers who had to choose between working sick and losing pay got nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding a new sick-pay mandate

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill during the H1N1 pandemic and referred it to the committee he chaired; it never advanced beyond a subcommittee referral.

for.name: 12 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote in two years, despite a Democratic majority and a Democratic committee chair as sponsor.

against.name: Employer and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed requiring employers to pay workers sent home sick, a recurring position in the broader fight over federal paid sick leave mandates in this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested on the floor; the bill's sponsor was the Democratic chairman of the committee that received it.

industries.industry: Employers without paid sick leave (especially hourly service-sector businesses)
industries.note: The bill would have required these employers to pay workers sent home with contagious symptoms for up to 5 days a year, a direct wage cost. Their interest in avoiding that mandate runs against workers' interest in being able to stay home sick without losing income.

industries.industry: Employers that already provide 5+ paid sick days
industries.note: These employers are explicitly exempt, so the bill imposes no new pay obligation on them. It levels the playing field against competitors that do not offer sick leave.

industries.industry: Hotels, restaurants, retail, and other public-facing sectors
industries.note: These employers would bear the pay cost most often, since their workers interact closely with customers, but their customers would face less exposure to sick employees. The public-health benefit and the labor cost fall on the same businesses.
